title: Introduce AWS SQS for decoupled communications in atlaspay-ledger
context: Direct HTTP calls between atlaspay-ledger and other services create hard dependencies. When downstream systems are down, transactions fail immediately, causing poor customer experience.
problem: Tight coupling leads to cascading failures across the backend. We need asynchronous messaging to guarantee eventual consistency and fault tolerance.
alternatives:
1. Keep synchronous REST APIs but increase timeouts and retry limits.
2. Introduce an HTTP webhook callback system.
3. Deploy AWS SQS as a centralized event broker.
decision: Integrate AWS SQS to enable asynchronous, event-driven communication between atlaspay-ledger and downstream microservices.
reason: By utilizing AWS SQS, we can queue tasks and process them asynchronously, absorbing sudden traffic spikes without affecting the main API transaction loop.
consequences: Requires handling out-of-order execution, ensuring message idempotency in processors, and setting up telemetry for queue lags.
expected_benefits: Cascading failures are avoided; service availability increases to 99.99%; peak traffic load is smoothed.
potential_risks: Introducing a single point of failure (event broker), message duplication, and increased complexity in tracing requests end-to-end.
outcome: Deployed in DEP-0041. Caused incident INC-0022 due to: Cache stampede in atlaspay-ledger for metadata queries. Rolled back or mitigated.

title: Implement Redis cache layer for security-scanner
context: security-scanner performs heavy database reads for static or slow-moving configurations, putting unnecessary read load on our primary databases and increasing endpoint latency.
problem: High load on databases and slow API responses due to repeated queries for the same static configuration and user profile data.
alternatives:
1. Add read replicas to the primary database.
2. Use in-memory application caching.
3. Deploy a centralized Redis caching cluster.
decision: Implement Redis as a distributed caching layer for security-scanner endpoints.
reason: A centralized Redis cluster allows shared cache across all horizontal pods of the service, keeping memory usage clean and providing sub-millisecond lookups.
consequences: Cache invalidation logic must be added to all update operations. Cache eviction policies (LRU) must be configured.
expected_benefits: Endpoint latency reduced by up to 80%; database read IOPS reduced by 60%.
potential_risks: Stale cache read anomalies, cache stampede during cold start, and additional cluster infrastructure costs.
outcome: Deployed in DEP-0066. Caused incident INC-0031 due to: Database connection pool exhaustion on security-scanner. Rolled back or mitigated.

title: Use Kubernetes to deploy platform-monitoring to AWS
context: Our current deployment model using manual VM provisioning is slow, error-prone, and makes scaling applications dynamically very difficult during high load.
problem: Deployment takes over 40 minutes, and we lack auto-scaling. Small configuration drift on VMs makes debugging environments difficult.
alternatives:
1. Script VM creation using custom Ansible and AMI images.
2. Deploy directly to AWS ECS.
3. Implement a complete Kubernetes container orchestration architecture.
decision: Standardize all microservice deployments, starting with platform-monitoring, on Kubernetes hosted on AWS.
reason: Kubernetes provides declarative configuration, auto-healing, and dynamic horizontal pod autoscaling (HPA) natively.
consequences: All services must be containerized (Dockerfiles written). Helm charts must be created, and CI/CD pipelines updated.
expected_benefits: Deployment time down from 40m to under 5m; auto-scaling responds to traffic load in under 2m.
potential_risks: Steep learning curve for the team, complex networking policies, and increased infrastructure cost for the control plane.
outcome: Deployed in DEP-0081. Caused incident INC-0039 due to: Message lag spike on Kafka partition for platform-monitoring. Rolled back or mitigated.

title: Adopt MongoDB for fusionerp-payroll database storage
context: Our current database strategy for fusionerp-payroll is experiencing scalability limitations under peak loads. We need a solution that can handle high throughput, support strong consistency, and scale horizontally.
problem: High read/write latency during peak traffic periods resulting in database connection pools exhausting, causing intermittent errors in downstream services.
alternatives:
1. Scale vertical resources on existing systems.
2. Implement a distributed cache layer (e.g. Redis) as a buffer.
3. Migrate to a multi-master distributed DB like MongoDB.
decision: Migrate the primary storage of fusionerp-payroll to MongoDB to leverage its native scaling and high availability features.
reason: We chose MongoDB because of its robust clustering capabilities, low latency reads, and strong developer familiarity. It provides the required performance profile and matches our tech stack.
consequences: Developers must learn MongoDB-specific query optimization. We must set up migration scripts and operational monitoring for the new clusters.
expected_benefits: Reduced query latency by 50%, elimination of connection pool exhaustion incidents, and support for 5x current transaction volume.
potential_risks: Complexity of live migration, operational overhead of maintaining clusters, and potential data format conversion issues during the transition.
outcome: Deployed in DEP-0106. Caused incident INC-0050 due to: Unoptimized query on fusionerp-payroll database after release. Rolled back or mitigated.

title: Introduce RabbitMQ for decoupled communications in atlaspay-gateway
context: Direct HTTP calls between atlaspay-gateway and other services create hard dependencies. When downstream systems are down, transactions fail immediately, causing poor customer experience.
problem: Tight coupling leads to cascading failures across the backend. We need asynchronous messaging to guarantee eventual consistency and fault tolerance.
alternatives:
1. Keep synchronous REST APIs but increase timeouts and retry limits.
2. Introduce an HTTP webhook callback system.
3. Deploy RabbitMQ as a centralized event broker.
decision: Integrate RabbitMQ to enable asynchronous, event-driven communication between atlaspay-gateway and downstream microservices.
reason: By utilizing RabbitMQ, we can queue tasks and process them asynchronously, absorbing sudden traffic spikes without affecting the main API transaction loop.
consequences: Requires handling out-of-order execution, ensuring message idempotency in processors, and setting up telemetry for queue lags.
expected_benefits: Cascading failures are avoided; service availability increases to 99.99%; peak traffic load is smoothed.
potential_risks: Introducing a single point of failure (event broker), message duplication, and increased complexity in tracing requests end-to-end.
outcome: Deployed in DEP-0521. Caused incident INC-0251 due to: Out of memory (OOM) crash in atlaspay-gateway pod during batch processing. Rolled back or mitigated.

problem: Bundle size is too large (5MB+), page interactive time (TTI) is over 6 seconds, and developers find it slow to build features.
alternatives:
1. Refactor the existing legacy code and optimize bundle sizes.
2. Migrate to Vanilla JS and web components.
3. Rebuild the frontend using Angular.
decision: Rebuild and migrate the UI for devops-ci-cd to Angular.
reason: Angular offers Server-Side Rendering (SSR) / Static Site Generation (SSG), excellent component ecosystem, and faster developer onboarding.
consequences: Full frontend rewrite is needed. Existing component libraries must be recreated or migrated.
expected_benefits: First Contentful Paint (FCP) improved from 4s to 1.2s; developer velocity increased.
potential_risks: Delays in feature parity during migration, state management refactoring challenges, and framework updates overhead.

title: Use Nomad to deploy security-scanner to AWS
context: Our current deployment model using manual VM provisioning is slow, error-prone, and makes scaling applications dynamically very difficult during high load.
problem: Deployment takes over 40 minutes, and we lack auto-scaling. Small configuration drift on VMs makes debugging environments difficult.
alternatives:
1. Script VM creation using custom Ansible and AMI images.
2. Deploy directly to AWS ECS.
3. Implement a complete Nomad container orchestration architecture.
decision: Standardize all microservice deployments, starting with security-scanner, on Nomad hosted on AWS.
reason: Nomad provides declarative configuration, auto-healing, and dynamic horizontal pod autoscaling (HPA) natively.
consequences: All services must be containerized (Dockerfiles written). Helm charts must be created, and CI/CD pipelines updated.
expected_benefits: Deployment time down from 40m to under 5m; auto-scaling responds to traffic load in under 2m.
potential_risks: Steep learning curve for the team, complex networking policies, and increased infrastructure cost for the control plane.

title: Adopt DynamoDB for security-scanner database storage
context: Our current database strategy for security-scanner is experiencing scalability limitations under peak loads. We need a solution that can handle high throughput, support strong consistency, and scale horizontally.
problem: High read/write latency during peak traffic periods resulting in database connection pools exhausting, causing intermittent errors in downstream services.
alternatives:
1. Scale vertical resources on existing systems.
2. Implement a distributed cache layer (e.g. Redis) as a buffer.
3. Migrate to a multi-master distributed DB like DynamoDB.
decision: Migrate the primary storage of security-scanner to DynamoDB to leverage its native scaling and high availability features.
reason: We chose DynamoDB because of its robust clustering capabilities, low latency reads, and strong developer familiarity. It provides the required performance profile and matches our tech stack.
consequences: Developers must learn DynamoDB-specific query optimization. We must set up migration scripts and operational monitoring for the new clusters.
expected_benefits: Reduced query latency by 50%, elimination of connection pool exhaustion incidents, and support for 5x current transaction volume.
potential_risks: Complexity of live migration, operational overhead of maintaining clusters, and potential data format conversion issues during the transition.

title: Introduce NATS for decoupled communications in insightcrm-api
context: Direct HTTP calls between insightcrm-api and other services create hard dependencies. When downstream systems are down, transactions fail immediately, causing poor customer experience.
problem: Tight coupling leads to cascading failures across the backend. We need asynchronous messaging to guarantee eventual consistency and fault tolerance.
alternatives:
1. Keep synchronous REST APIs but increase timeouts and retry limits.
2. Introduce an HTTP webhook callback system.
3. Deploy NATS as a centralized event broker.
decision: Integrate NATS to enable asynchronous, event-driven communication between insightcrm-api and downstream microservices.
reason: By utilizing NATS, we can queue tasks and process them asynchronously, absorbing sudden traffic spikes without affecting the main API transaction loop.
consequences: Requires handling out-of-order execution, ensuring message idempotency in processors, and setting up telemetry for queue lags.
expected_benefits: Cascading failures are avoided; service availability increases to 99.99%; peak traffic load is smoothed.
potential_risks: Introducing a single point of failure (event broker), message duplication, and increased complexity in tracing requests end-to-end.

title: Implement Redis cache layer for novacommerce-ui
context: novacommerce-ui performs heavy database reads for static or slow-moving configurations, putting unnecessary read load on our primary databases and increasing endpoint latency.
problem: High load on databases and slow API responses due to repeated queries for the same static configuration and user profile data.
alternatives:
1. Add read replicas to the primary database.
2. Use in-memory application caching.
3. Deploy a centralized Redis caching cluster.
decision: Implement Redis as a distributed caching layer for novacommerce-ui endpoints.
reason: A centralized Redis cluster allows shared cache across all horizontal pods of the service, keeping memory usage clean and providing sub-millisecond lookups.
consequences: Cache invalidation logic must be added to all update operations. Cache eviction policies (LRU) must be configured.
expected_benefits: Endpoint latency reduced by up to 80%; database read IOPS reduced by 60%.
potential_risks: Stale cache read anomalies, cache stampede during cold start, and additional cluster infrastructure costs.

title: Introduce Kafka for decoupled communications in visionai-training

decision: Integrate Kafka to enable asynchronous, event-driven communication between visionai-training and downstream microservices.
reason: By utilizing Kafka, we can queue tasks and process them asynchronously, absorbing sudden traffic spikes without affecting the main API transaction loop.
consequences: Requires handling out-of-order execution, ensuring message idempotency in processors, and setting up telemetry for queue lags.
expected_benefits: Cascading failures are avoided; service availability increases to 99.99%; peak traffic load is smoothed.
potential_risks: Introducing a single point of failure (event broker), message duplication, and increased complexity in tracing requests end-to-end.

title: Introduce RabbitMQ for decoupled communications in cloudsync-storage
context: Direct HTTP calls between cloudsync-storage and other services create hard dependencies. When downstream systems are down, transactions fail immediately, causing poor customer experience.
problem: Tight coupling leads to cascading failures across the backend. We need asynchronous messaging to guarantee eventual consistency and fault tolerance.
alternatives:
1. Keep synchronous REST APIs but increase timeouts and retry limits.
2. Introduce an HTTP webhook callback system.
3. Deploy RabbitMQ as a centralized event broker.
decision: Integrate RabbitMQ to enable asynchronous, event-driven communication between cloudsync-storage and downstream microservices.
reason: By utilizing RabbitMQ, we can queue tasks and process them asynchronously, absorbing sudden traffic spikes without affecting the main API transaction loop.
consequences: Requires handling out-of-order execution, ensuring message idempotency in processors, and setting up telemetry for queue lags.
expected_benefits: Cascading failures are avoided; service availability increases to 99.99%; peak traffic load is smoothed.
potential_risks: Introducing a single point of failure (event broker), message duplication, and increased complexity in tracing requests end-to-end.

title: Implement Memcached cache layer for security-auth-proxy
context: security-auth-proxy performs heavy database reads for static or slow-moving configurations, putting unnecessary read load on our primary databases and increasing endpoint latency.
problem: High load on databases and slow API responses due to repeated queries for the same static configuration and user profile data.
alternatives:
1. Add read replicas to the primary database.
2. Use in-memory application caching.
3. Deploy a centralized Memcached caching cluster.
decision: Implement Memcached as a distributed caching layer for security-auth-proxy endpoints.
reason: A centralized Memcached cluster allows shared cache across all horizontal pods of the service, keeping memory usage clean and providing sub-millisecond lookups.
consequences: Cache invalidation logic must be added to all update operations. Cache eviction policies (LRU) must be configured.
expected_benefits: Endpoint latency reduced by up to 80%; database read IOPS reduced by 60%.
potential_risks: Stale cache read anomalies, cache stampede during cold start, and additional cluster infrastructure costs.

title: Implement Redis cache layer for insightcrm-api
context: insightcrm-api performs heavy database reads for static or slow-moving configurations, putting unnecessary read load on our primary databases and increasing endpoint latency.
problem: High load on databases and slow API responses due to repeated queries for the same static configuration and user profile data.
alternatives:
1. Add read replicas to the primary database.
2. Use in-memory application caching.
3. Deploy a centralized Redis caching cluster.
decision: Implement Redis as a distributed caching layer for insightcrm-api endpoints.
reason: A centralized Redis cluster allows shared cache across all horizontal pods of the service, keeping memory usage clean and providing sub-millisecond lookups.
consequences: Cache invalidation logic must be added to all update operations. Cache eviction policies (LRU) must be configured.
expected_benefits: Endpoint latency reduced by up to 80%; database read IOPS reduced by 60%.
potential_risks: Stale cache read anomalies, cache stampede during cold start, and additional cluster infrastructure costs.

title: Introduce NATS for decoupled communications in security-auth-proxy
context: Direct HTTP calls between security-auth-proxy and other services create hard dependencies. When downstream systems are down, transactions fail immediately, causing poor customer experience.
problem: Tight coupling leads to cascading failures across the backend. We need asynchronous messaging to guarantee eventual consistency and fault tolerance.
alternatives:
1. Keep synchronous REST APIs but increase timeouts and retry limits.
2. Introduce an HTTP webhook callback system.
3. Deploy NATS as a centralized event broker.
decision: Integrate NATS to enable asynchronous, event-driven communication between security-auth-proxy and downstream microservices.
reason: By utilizing NATS, we can queue tasks and process them asynchronously, absorbing sudden traffic spikes without affecting the main API transaction loop.
consequences: Requires handling out-of-order execution, ensuring message idempotency in processors, and setting up telemetry for queue lags.
expected_benefits: Cascading failures are avoided; service availability increases to 99.99%; peak traffic load is smoothed.
potential_risks: Introducing a single point of failure (event broker), message duplication, and increased complexity in tracing requests end-to-end.

title: Migrate platform-monitoring frontend architecture to Vue.js
context: The legacy user interface of platform-monitoring is written in a monolithic, unmaintained framework. It leads to slow page loads, poor SEO, and difficulty in writing modern components.
problem: Bundle size is too large (5MB+), page interactive time (TTI) is over 6 seconds, and developers find it slow to build features.
alternatives:
1. Refactor the existing legacy code and optimize bundle sizes.
2. Migrate to Vanilla JS and web components.
3. Rebuild the frontend using Vue.js.
decision: Rebuild and migrate the UI for platform-monitoring to Vue.js.
reason: Vue.js offers Server-Side Rendering (SSR) / Static Site Generation (SSG), excellent component ecosystem, and faster developer onboarding.
consequences: Full frontend rewrite is needed. Existing component libraries must be recreated or migrated.
expected_benefits: First Contentful Paint (FCP) improved from 4s to 1.2s; developer velocity increased.
potential_risks: Delays in feature parity during migration, state management refactoring challenges, and framework updates overhead.

title: Introduce RabbitMQ for decoupled communications in fusionerp-frontend
context: Direct HTTP calls between fusionerp-frontend and other services create hard dependencies. When downstream systems are down, transactions fail immediately, causing poor customer experience.
problem: Tight coupling leads to cascading failures across the backend. We need asynchronous messaging to guarantee eventual consistency and fault tolerance.
alternatives:
1. Keep synchronous REST APIs but increase timeouts and retry limits.
2. Introduce an HTTP webhook callback system.
3. Deploy RabbitMQ as a centralized event broker.
decision: Integrate RabbitMQ to enable asynchronous, event-driven communication between fusionerp-frontend and downstream microservices.
reason: By utilizing RabbitMQ, we can queue tasks and process them asynchronously, absorbing sudden traffic spikes without affecting the main API transaction loop.
consequences: Requires handling out-of-order execution, ensuring message idempotency in processors, and setting up telemetry for queue lags.
expected_benefits: Cascading failures are avoided; service availability increases to 99.99%; peak traffic load is smoothed.
potential_risks: Introducing a single point of failure (event broker), message duplication, and increased complexity in tracing requests end-to-end.

title: Adopt MySQL for security-auth-proxy database storage
context: Our current database strategy for security-auth-proxy is experiencing scalability limitations under peak loads. We need a solution that can handle high throughput, support strong consistency, and scale horizontally.
problem: High read/write latency during peak traffic periods resulting in database connection pools exhausting, causing intermittent errors in downstream services.
alternatives:
1. Scale vertical resources on existing systems.
2. Implement a distributed cache layer (e.g. Redis) as a buffer.
3. Migrate to a multi-master distributed DB like MySQL.
decision: Migrate the primary storage of security-auth-proxy to MySQL to leverage its native scaling and high availability features.
reason: We chose MySQL because of its robust clustering capabilities, low latency reads, and strong developer familiarity. It provides the required performance profile and matches our tech stack.
consequences: Developers must learn MySQL-specific query optimization. We must set up migration scripts and operational monitoring for the new clusters.
expected_benefits: Reduced query latency by 50%, elimination of connection pool exhaustion incidents, and support for 5x current transaction volume.
potential_risks: Complexity of live migration, operational overhead of maintaining clusters, and potential data format conversion issues during the transition.

title: Use Nomad to deploy atlaspay-portal to AWS
context: Our current deployment model using manual VM provisioning is slow, error-prone, and makes scaling applications dynamically very difficult during high load.
problem: Deployment takes over 40 minutes, and we lack auto-scaling. Small configuration drift on VMs makes debugging environments difficult.
alternatives:
1. Script VM creation using custom Ansible and AMI images.
2. Deploy directly to AWS ECS.
3. Implement a complete Nomad container orchestration architecture.
decision: Standardize all microservice deployments, starting with atlaspay-portal, on Nomad hosted on AWS.
reason: Nomad provides declarative configuration, auto-healing, and dynamic horizontal pod autoscaling (HPA) natively.
consequences: All services must be containerized (Dockerfiles written). Helm charts must be created, and CI/CD pipelines updated.
expected_benefits: Deployment time down from 40m to under 5m; auto-scaling responds to traffic load in under 2m.
potential_risks: Steep learning curve for the team, complex networking policies, and increased infrastructure cost for the control plane.

title: Implement Memcached cache layer for insightcrm-analytics
context: insightcrm-analytics performs heavy database reads for static or slow-moving configurations, putting unnecessary read load on our primary databases and increasing endpoint latency.
problem: High load on databases and slow API responses due to repeated queries for the same static configuration and user profile data.
alternatives:
1. Add read replicas to the primary database.
2. Use in-memory application caching.
3. Deploy a centralized Memcached caching cluster.
decision: Implement Memcached as a distributed caching layer for insightcrm-analytics endpoints.
reason: A centralized Memcached cluster allows shared cache across all horizontal pods of the service, keeping memory usage clean and providing sub-millisecond lookups.
consequences: Cache invalidation logic must be added to all update operations. Cache eviction policies (LRU) must be configured.
expected_benefits: Endpoint latency reduced by up to 80%; database read IOPS reduced by 60%.
potential_risks: Stale cache read anomalies, cache stampede during cold start, and additional cluster infrastructure costs.

title: Introduce NATS for decoupled communications in cloudsync-daemon
context: Direct HTTP calls between cloudsync-daemon and other services create hard dependencies. When downstream systems are down, transactions fail immediately, causing poor customer experience.
problem: Tight coupling leads to cascading failures across the backend. We need asynchronous messaging to guarantee eventual consistency and fault tolerance.
alternatives:
1. Keep synchronous REST APIs but increase timeouts and retry limits.
2. Introduce an HTTP webhook callback system.
3. Deploy NATS as a centralized event broker.
decision: Integrate NATS to enable asynchronous, event-driven communication between cloudsync-daemon and downstream microservices.
reason: By utilizing NATS, we can queue tasks and process them asynchronously, absorbing sudden traffic spikes without affecting the main API transaction loop.
consequences: Requires handling out-of-order execution, ensuring message idempotency in processors, and setting up telemetry for queue lags.
expected_benefits: Cascading failures are avoided; service availability increases to 99.99%; peak traffic load is smoothed.
potential_risks: Introducing a single point of failure (event broker), message duplication, and increased complexity in tracing requests end-to-end.

title: Adopt PostgreSQL for cloudsync-daemon database storage
context: Our current database strategy for cloudsync-daemon is experiencing scalability limitations under peak loads. We need a solution that can handle high throughput, support strong consistency, and scale horizontally.
problem: High read/write latency during peak traffic periods resulting in database connection pools exhausting, causing intermittent errors in downstream services.
alternatives:
1. Scale vertical resources on existing systems.
2. Implement a distributed cache layer (e.g. Redis) as a buffer.
3. Migrate to a multi-master distributed DB like PostgreSQL.
decision: Migrate the primary storage of cloudsync-daemon to PostgreSQL to leverage its native scaling and high availability features.
reason: We chose PostgreSQL because of its robust clustering capabilities, low latency reads, and strong developer familiarity. It provides the required performance profile and matches our tech stack.
consequences: Developers must learn PostgreSQL-specific query optimization. We must set up migration scripts and operational monitoring for the new clusters.
expected_benefits: Reduced query latency by 50%, elimination of connection pool exhaustion incidents, and support for 5x current transaction volume.
potential_risks: Complexity of live migration, operational overhead of maintaining clusters, and potential data format conversion issues during the transition.

title: Adopt DynamoDB for novacommerce-cart database storage
context: Our current database strategy for novacommerce-cart is experiencing scalability limitations under peak loads. We need a solution that can handle high throughput, support strong consistency, and scale horizontally.
problem: High read/write latency during peak traffic periods resulting in database connection pools exhausting, causing intermittent errors in downstream services.
alternatives:
1. Scale vertical resources on existing systems.
2. Implement a distributed cache layer (e.g. Redis) as a buffer.
3. Migrate to a multi-master distributed DB like DynamoDB.
decision: Migrate the primary storage of novacommerce-cart to DynamoDB to leverage its native scaling and high availability features.
reason: We chose DynamoDB because of its robust clustering capabilities, low latency reads, and strong developer familiarity. It provides the required performance profile and matches our tech stack.
consequences: Developers must learn DynamoDB-specific query optimization. We must set up migration scripts and operational monitoring for the new clusters.
expected_benefits: Reduced query latency by 50%, elimination of connection pool exhaustion incidents, and support for 5x current transaction volume.
potential_risks: Complexity of live migration, operational overhead of maintaining clusters, and potential data format conversion issues during the transition.

title: Implement Redis cache layer for atlaspay-ledger
context: atlaspay-ledger performs heavy database reads for static or slow-moving configurations, putting unnecessary read load on our primary databases and increasing endpoint latency.
problem: High load on databases and slow API responses due to repeated queries for the same static configuration and user profile data.
alternatives:
1. Add read replicas to the primary database.
2. Use in-memory application caching.
3. Deploy a centralized Redis caching cluster.
decision: Implement Redis as a distributed caching layer for atlaspay-ledger endpoints.
reason: A centralized Redis cluster allows shared cache across all horizontal pods of the service, keeping memory usage clean and providing sub-millisecond lookups.
consequences: Cache invalidation logic must be added to all update operations. Cache eviction policies (LRU) must be configured.
expected_benefits: Endpoint latency reduced by up to 80%; database read IOPS reduced by 60%.
potential_risks: Stale cache read anomalies, cache stampede during cold start, and additional cluster infrastructure costs.

title: Introduce Kafka for decoupled communications in atlaspay-ledger
context: Direct HTTP calls between atlaspay-ledger and other services create hard dependencies. When downstream systems are down, transactions fail immediately, causing poor customer experience.
problem: Tight coupling leads to cascading failures across the backend. We need asynchronous messaging to guarantee eventual consistency and fault tolerance.
alternatives:
1. Keep synchronous REST APIs but increase timeouts and retry limits.
2. Introduce an HTTP webhook callback system.
3. Deploy Kafka as a centralized event broker.
decision: Integrate Kafka to enable asynchronous, event-driven communication between atlaspay-ledger and downstream microservices.
reason: By utilizing Kafka, we can queue tasks and process them asynchronously, absorbing sudden traffic spikes without affecting the main API transaction loop.
consequences: Requires handling out-of-order execution, ensuring message idempotency in processors, and setting up telemetry for queue lags.
expected_benefits: Cascading failures are avoided; service availability increases to 99.99%; peak traffic load is smoothed.
potential_risks: Introducing a single point of failure (event broker), message duplication, and increased complexity in tracing requests end-to-end.

title: Migrate cloudsync-desktop frontend architecture to Vue.js
context: The legacy user interface of cloudsync-desktop is written in a monolithic, unmaintained framework. It leads to slow page loads, poor SEO, and difficulty in writing modern components.
problem: Bundle size is too large (5MB+), page interactive time (TTI) is over 6 seconds, and developers find it slow to build features.
alternatives:
1. Refactor the existing legacy code and optimize bundle sizes.
2. Migrate to Vanilla JS and web components.
3. Rebuild the frontend using Vue.js.
decision: Rebuild and migrate the UI for cloudsync-desktop to Vue.js.
reason: Vue.js offers Server-Side Rendering (SSR) / Static Site Generation (SSG), excellent component ecosystem, and faster developer onboarding.
consequences: Full frontend rewrite is needed. Existing component libraries must be recreated or migrated.
expected_benefits: First Contentful Paint (FCP) improved from 4s to 1.2s; developer velocity increased.
potential_risks: Delays in feature parity during migration, state management refactoring challenges, and framework updates overhead.

title: Implement Memcached cache layer for insightcrm-ui
context: insightcrm-ui performs heavy database reads for static or slow-moving configurations, putting unnecessary read load on our primary databases and increasing endpoint latency.

decision: Implement Memcached as a distributed caching layer for insightcrm-ui endpoints.

title: Introduce RabbitMQ for decoupled communications in insightcrm-analytics
context: Direct HTTP calls between insightcrm-analytics and other services create hard dependencies. When downstream systems are down, transactions fail immediately, causing poor customer experience.
problem: Tight coupling leads to cascading failures across the backend. We need asynchronous messaging to guarantee eventual consistency and fault tolerance.
alternatives:
1. Keep synchronous REST APIs but increase timeouts and retry limits.
2. Introduce an HTTP webhook callback system.
3. Deploy RabbitMQ as a centralized event broker.
decision: Integrate RabbitMQ to enable asynchronous, event-driven communication between insightcrm-analytics and downstream microservices.
reason: By utilizing RabbitMQ, we can queue tasks and process them asynchronously, absorbing sudden traffic spikes without affecting the main API transaction loop.
consequences: Requires handling out-of-order execution, ensuring message idempotency in processors, and setting up telemetry for queue lags.
expected_benefits: Cascading failures are avoided; service availability increases to 99.99%; peak traffic load is smoothed.
potential_risks: Introducing a single point of failure (event broker), message duplication, and increased complexity in tracing requests end-to-end.

title: Introduce RabbitMQ for decoupled communications in platform-k8s-mesh

title: Adopt MongoDB for novacommerce-checkout database storage

consequences: Developers must learn MongoDB-specific query optimization. We must set up migration scripts and operational monitoring for the new clusters.
expected_benefits: Reduced query latency by 50%, elimination of connection pool exhaustion incidents, and support for 5x current transaction volume.
potential_risks: Complexity of live migration, operational overhead of maintaining clusters, and potential data format conversion issues during the transition.

title: Introduce AWS SQS for decoupled communications in visionai-pipeline
context: Direct HTTP calls between visionai-pipeline and other services create hard dependencies. When downstream systems are down, transactions fail immediately, causing poor customer experience.
problem: Tight coupling leads to cascading failures across the backend. We need asynchronous messaging to guarantee eventual consistency and fault tolerance.
alternatives:
1. Keep synchronous REST APIs but increase timeouts and retry limits.
2. Introduce an HTTP webhook callback system.
3. Deploy AWS SQS as a centralized event broker.
decision: Integrate AWS SQS to enable asynchronous, event-driven communication between visionai-pipeline and downstream microservices.
reason: By utilizing AWS SQS, we can queue tasks and process them asynchronously, absorbing sudden traffic spikes without affecting the main API transaction loop.
consequences: Requires handling out-of-order execution, ensuring message idempotency in processors, and setting up telemetry for queue lags.
expected_benefits: Cascading failures are avoided; service availability increases to 99.99%; peak traffic load is smoothed.
potential_risks: Introducing a single point of failure (event broker), message duplication, and increased complexity in tracing requests end-to-end.

title: Implement Memcached cache layer for fusionerp-frontend
context: fusionerp-frontend performs heavy database reads for static or slow-moving configurations, putting unnecessary read load on our primary databases and increasing endpoint latency.
problem: High load on databases and slow API responses due to repeated queries for the same static configuration and user profile data.
alternatives:
1. Add read replicas to the primary database.
2. Use in-memory application caching.
3. Deploy a centralized Memcached caching cluster.
decision: Implement Memcached as a distributed caching layer for fusionerp-frontend endpoints.
reason: A centralized Memcached cluster allows shared cache across all horizontal pods of the service, keeping memory usage clean and providing sub-millisecond lookups.
consequences: Cache invalidation logic must be added to all update operations. Cache eviction policies (LRU) must be configured.
expected_benefits: Endpoint latency reduced by up to 80%; database read IOPS reduced by 60%.
potential_risks: Stale cache read anomalies, cache stampede during cold start, and additional cluster infrastructure costs.

title: Introduce RabbitMQ for decoupled communications in cloudsync-daemon
context: Direct HTTP calls between cloudsync-daemon and other services create hard dependencies. When downstream systems are down, transactions fail immediately, causing poor customer experience.
problem: Tight coupling leads to cascading failures across the backend. We need asynchronous messaging to guarantee eventual consistency and fault tolerance.
alternatives:
1. Keep synchronous REST APIs but increase timeouts and retry limits.
2. Introduce an HTTP webhook callback system.
3. Deploy RabbitMQ as a centralized event broker.
decision: Integrate RabbitMQ to enable asynchronous, event-driven communication between cloudsync-daemon and downstream microservices.
reason: By utilizing RabbitMQ, we can queue tasks and process them asynchronously, absorbing sudden traffic spikes without affecting the main API transaction loop.
consequences: Requires handling out-of-order execution, ensuring message idempotency in processors, and setting up telemetry for queue lags.
expected_benefits: Cascading failures are avoided; service availability increases to 99.99%; peak traffic load is smoothed.
potential_risks: Introducing a single point of failure (event broker), message duplication, and increased complexity in tracing requests end-to-end.

problem: Bundle size is too large (5MB+), page interactive time (TTI) is over 6 seconds, and developers find it slow to build features.
alternatives:
1. Refactor the existing legacy code and optimize bundle sizes.
2. Migrate to Vanilla JS and web components.
3. Rebuild the frontend using React / Next.js.
decision: Rebuild and migrate the UI for novacommerce-ui to React / Next.js.
reason: React / Next.js offers Server-Side Rendering (SSR) / Static Site Generation (SSG), excellent component ecosystem, and faster developer onboarding.
consequences: Full frontend rewrite is needed. Existing component libraries must be recreated or migrated.
expected_benefits: First Contentful Paint (FCP) improved from 4s to 1.2s; developer velocity increased.
potential_risks: Delays in feature parity during migration, state management refactoring challenges, and framework updates overhead.

title: Use Kubernetes to deploy platform-monitoring to AWS
context: Our current deployment model using manual VM provisioning is slow, error-prone, and makes scaling applications dynamically very difficult during high load.
problem: Deployment takes over 40 minutes, and we lack auto-scaling. Small configuration drift on VMs makes debugging environments difficult.
alternatives:
1. Script VM creation using custom Ansible and AMI images.
2. Deploy directly to AWS ECS.
3. Implement a complete Kubernetes container orchestration architecture.
decision: Standardize all microservice deployments, starting with platform-monitoring, on Kubernetes hosted on AWS.
reason: Kubernetes provides declarative configuration, auto-healing, and dynamic horizontal pod autoscaling (HPA) natively.
consequences: All services must be containerized (Dockerfiles written). Helm charts must be created, and CI/CD pipelines updated.
expected_benefits: Deployment time down from 40m to under 5m; auto-scaling responds to traffic load in under 2m.
potential_risks: Steep learning curve for the team, complex networking policies, and increased infrastructure cost for the control plane.

title: Introduce NATS for decoupled communications in security-scanner
context: Direct HTTP calls between security-scanner and other services create hard dependencies. When downstream systems are down, transactions fail immediately, causing poor customer experience.
problem: Tight coupling leads to cascading failures across the backend. We need asynchronous messaging to guarantee eventual consistency and fault tolerance.
alternatives:
1. Keep synchronous REST APIs but increase timeouts and retry limits.
2. Introduce an HTTP webhook callback system.
3. Deploy NATS as a centralized event broker.
decision: Integrate NATS to enable asynchronous, event-driven communication between security-scanner and downstream microservices.
reason: By utilizing NATS, we can queue tasks and process them asynchronously, absorbing sudden traffic spikes without affecting the main API transaction loop.
consequences: Requires handling out-of-order execution, ensuring message idempotency in processors, and setting up telemetry for queue lags.
expected_benefits: Cascading failures are avoided; service availability increases to 99.99%; peak traffic load is smoothed.
potential_risks: Introducing a single point of failure (event broker), message duplication, and increased complexity in tracing requests end-to-end.

title: Implement Memcached cache layer for atlaspay-ledger
context: atlaspay-ledger performs heavy database reads for static or slow-moving configurations, putting unnecessary read load on our primary databases and increasing endpoint latency.
problem: High load on databases and slow API responses due to repeated queries for the same static configuration and user profile data.
alternatives:
1. Add read replicas to the primary database.
2. Use in-memory application caching.
3. Deploy a centralized Memcached caching cluster.
decision: Implement Memcached as a distributed caching layer for atlaspay-ledger endpoints.
reason: A centralized Memcached cluster allows shared cache across all horizontal pods of the service, keeping memory usage clean and providing sub-millisecond lookups.
consequences: Cache invalidation logic must be added to all update operations. Cache eviction policies (LRU) must be configured.
expected_benefits: Endpoint latency reduced by up to 80%; database read IOPS reduced by 60%.
potential_risks: Stale cache read anomalies, cache stampede during cold start, and additional cluster infrastructure costs.

title: Adopt DynamoDB for atlaspay-gateway database storage
context: Our current database strategy for atlaspay-gateway is experiencing scalability limitations under peak loads. We need a solution that can handle high throughput, support strong consistency, and scale horizontally.
problem: High read/write latency during peak traffic periods resulting in database connection pools exhausting, causing intermittent errors in downstream services.
alternatives:
1. Scale vertical resources on existing systems.
2. Implement a distributed cache layer (e.g. Redis) as a buffer.
3. Migrate to a multi-master distributed DB like DynamoDB.
decision: Migrate the primary storage of atlaspay-gateway to DynamoDB to leverage its native scaling and high availability features.
reason: We chose DynamoDB because of its robust clustering capabilities, low latency reads, and strong developer familiarity. It provides the required performance profile and matches our tech stack.
consequences: Developers must learn DynamoDB-specific query optimization. We must set up migration scripts and operational monitoring for the new clusters.
expected_benefits: Reduced query latency by 50%, elimination of connection pool exhaustion incidents, and support for 5x current transaction volume.
potential_risks: Complexity of live migration, operational overhead of maintaining clusters, and potential data format conversion issues during the transition.
